# Diode rectifiers

*Lecture 1 · EEU 08104 Power Electronics Design*

Diode rectifiers give a fixed DC output. Throughout, the supply is $v_s = V_m \sin\omega t$ with $V_m = \sqrt2\,V_s$, and the diodes are ideal (zero voltage when conducting).

m">v<tspan dy="4" font-size="10">s</tspan><tspan dy="-4"> (dashed)</tspan></text></svg><figcaption>Half-wave diode rectifier, resistive load. The load sees only the positive half cycles; the diode blocks the negative ones, so V<sub>dc</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/π.</figcaption></figure>

**Circuit equation:** $v_s = v_D + v_R$.

- **Positive half cycle:** the diode is forward biased, so $v_D = 0$ (the anode–cathode voltage of a conducting diode is taken as zero). Then $v_R = v_s$ and $i = V_m \sin\omega t / R$.
- **Negative half cycle:** the diode is reverse biased, $i = 0$, $v_R = 0$ and the whole supply appears across the diode: $v_D = v_s$. The **peak inverse voltage** is $V_m$.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Peak current | $I_m = V_m/R$ |
| Average voltage | $V_{dc} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} V_m \sin\omega t\, d(\omega t) = \dfrac{V_m}{\pi} = 0.318V_m$ |
| Average current | $I_{dc} = I_m/\pi$ |
| rms voltage | $V_{rms} = V_m/2$ |
| rms current | $I_{rms} = I_m/2$ |

## Single-phase half-wave, RL load

Most practical loads are inductive. With an RL load the circuit equation is $v_s = v_L + v_R + v_D$, and while the diode conducts

$$\sqrt2 V_s \sin\omega t = L\frac{di}{dt} + Ri$$

With $i = 0$ at $t = 0$, the solution is

$$i(\omega t) = \frac{V_m}{Z}\left[\sin(\omega t - \theta) + \sin\theta\; e^{-\omega t/\tan\theta}\right]$$

$$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (\omega L)^2}, \qquad \theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{\omega L}{R}, \qquad \omega = 2\pi f$$

The exponent can also be written $-Rt/L$, since $\omega t/\tan\theta = Rt/L$.

m">π</text><line x1="300.0" y1="136" x2="300.0" y2="144" class="d-ax" /><text x="300.0" y="160" text-anchor="middle" class="d-t s m">2π</text><text x="120" y="40" text-anchor="middle" class="d-t s a">v<tspan dy="4" font-size="10">o</tspan></text><text x="225" y="80" text-anchor="middle" class="d-t s b">i<tspan dy="4" font-size="10">o</tspan></text><text x="380" y="70" text-anchor="start" class="d-t s m">The diode keeps conducting after π</text><text x="380" y="88" text-anchor="start" class="d-t s m">until i falls to zero at β,</text><text x="380" y="106" text-anchor="start" class="d-t s m">so v<tspan dy="4" font-size="10">o</tspan><tspan dy="-4"> goes negative.</tspan></text></svg><figcaption>Half-wave diode rectifier with an RL load (φ = 50°). Stored inductor energy keeps the diode on past π, to the extinction angle β, so part of the negative half cycle reaches the load.</figcaption></figure>

- The inductor stores energy while the current rises. After $\omega t = \pi$ it keeps the diode conducting until the current reaches zero at the **extinction angle** $\beta$ (found by setting $i(\beta) = 0$, numerically).
- From $\pi$ to $\beta$ the load sees part of the **negative** half cycle, so the average voltage is lower than with a resistive load:

$$V_{dc} = \frac{V_m}{2\pi}\,(1 - \cos\beta)$$

In the positive half cycle current flows D1 → load → D2; in the negative half cycle D3 → load → D4. The load current is always in the same direction.</figcaption></figure>

- **First half cycle:** current flows from the source through **D1 → load → D2** and back to the source.
- **Second half cycle:** current flows through **D3 → load → D4**.
- The load current is in the same direction in both halves, so current flows in the load during the second half cycle too.

y1="126" x2="540.0" y2="134" class="d-ax" /><text x="540.0" y="150" text-anchor="middle" class="d-t s m">4π</text></svg><figcaption>Full-wave bridge output with a resistive load. Both half cycles reach the load in the same direction, doubling the average voltage to 2V<sub>m</sub>/π.</figcaption></figure>

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Average current | $I_{av} = \dfrac{1}{T}\displaystyle\int_0^T i_L(t)\,dt = \dfrac{2I_m}{\pi}$ |
| Average voltage | $V_{av} = \dfrac{2V_m}{\pi} = 0.637V_m$ |
| rms current | $I_{rms} = \left[\dfrac{1}{T}\displaystyle\int_0^T i_L^2\,dt\right]^{1/2} = \dfrac{I_m}{\sqrt2}$ |
| rms voltage | $V_{rms} = V_m/\sqrt2$ |

Each diode must block the full peak $V_m$ in its off half cycle.

## Three-phase bridge rectifier

- It is a **full-wave** rectifier with six diodes. **Each diode conducts for 120°.**
- At any instant, the pair of diodes connected between the pair of supply lines with the **highest instantaneous line-to-line voltage** conducts: one from the top group (D1, D3, D5) and one from the bottom group (D4, D6, D2).
- The line-to-line voltage is $\sqrt3 V_m \sin\omega t$, where $V_m$ is the **peak phase voltage**.

x1="540.0" y1="226" x2="540.0" y2="234" class="d-ax" /><text x="540.0" y="250" text-anchor="middle" class="d-t s m">4π</text></svg><figcaption>Three-phase diode bridge output (bold): at every instant the largest line-to-line voltage reaches the load, giving six pulses per cycle and V<sub>dc</sub> = 3√3V<sub>m</sub>/π = 1.654V<sub>m</sub>.</figcaption></figure>

Each of the six pulses lasts 60° ($\pi/3$), centred on a peak of the line voltage, so

$$V_{dc} = \frac{1}{\pi/3}\int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3} \sqrt3 V_m \sin\omega t\; d(\omega t) = \frac{3\sqrt3}{\pi}V_m = 1.654V_m$$

$$V_{rms} = \left[\frac{1}{\pi/3}\int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3} 3V_m^2 \sin^2\omega t\; d(\omega t)\right]^{1/2} = 1.6554V_m$$

The output ripple is small: the rms value is only 0.08% above the average.

**Currents, purely resistive load.** The peak line current is $I_m = \sqrt3 V_m/R$.

| Current | Value |
|---|---|
| Average diode current | $I_d = \dfrac{4}{2\pi}\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/6} I_m \cos\omega t\, d(\omega t) = \dfrac{I_m}{\pi} = 0.3183I_m$ (also $= I_{dc}/3$) |
| rms diode current | $I_{d,rms} = \left[\dfrac{2}{2\pi}\displaystyle\int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3} I_m^2 \sin^2\omega t\, d(\omega t)\right]^{1/2} = 0.5518I_m$ |
| rms transformer secondary (line) current | $I_s = \left[\dfrac{4}{2\pi}\displaystyle\int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3} I_m^2\sin^2\omega t\, d(\omega t)\right]^{1/2} = 0.7804I_m$ |

**Peak inverse voltage** of each diode: the peak line voltage, $PIV = \sqrt3 V_m$.

### Worked example: three-phase bridge with a resistive load

*A three-phase bridge rectifier has a purely resistive load R and delivers $I_{dc} = 60$ A at $V_{dc} = 280.7$ V from a 50 Hz supply. Find (a) the efficiency, (b) the PIV of each diode, (c) the average and peak current through a diode.*

**(a)** $R = 280.7/60 = 4.678\ \Omega$. $P_{dc} = 60 \times 280.7 = 16\,842$ W. $V_m = 280.7/1.654 = 169.7$ V, so $V_{rms} = 1.6554 \times 169.7 = 280.9$ V and $P_{ac} = V_{rms}^2/R = 16\,870$ W.

$$\eta = \frac{P_{dc}}{P_{ac}} = \frac{16\,842}{16\,870} = 99.83\%$$

**(b)** $PIV = \sqrt3 V_m = \sqrt3 \times 169.7 = 293.9$ V.

**(c)** Average diode current $I_d = 60/3 = 20$ A. Since $I_d = 0.3183I_m$, the peak diode current is $I_m = 20/0.3183 = 62.83$ A (check: $\sqrt3 \times 169.7/4.678 = 62.83$ A).

> **Corrections to the lecture slides.** The worked solution labels its parts (e) and (f), but the question only has parts (a) to (c). On the slide for the average diode current, the factor in front of the integral is written $1/T$ with limits $0$ to $\pi/6$; it should be $4/2\pi$ (in its 120° conduction the diode carries two 60° segments, each spanning $\pm\pi/6$ about a peak, giving four integrals from $0$ to $\pi/6$ per cycle), which gives the stated $I_m/\pi = 0.3183I_m$.
